items.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005
items.q: who ever thought that in 1936 I would become the lead alto man in New York with Paul Whiteman?

ctx.x: Yeah. It must have been hard for you to see some of that devastation that happened with Katrina, having lived there for a while.

We were always — the Italians and Birmingham and Inslee, we got along. There was no — But I have to tell you this story. It must have been early 1928. See I moved to New Orleans from Birmingham or Pensacola, Florida, October of ’27. It could have been late ’27 or early ’28 the St. Charles Theater on St. Charles Street — there’s an Avenue and a Street — The Paul Whiteman Band was coming through. And God I’m only about 15 years old, fifteen and a half years old. And I waited outside and who gets out of a cab? The…
Why did you know — why was he sort of an idol for you at that time? Through radio or through purchasing his records or what?

items.title: Spiegle Willcox and Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Norwich, New York, November 14, 1995
items.q: I signed a contract and I was with the Whiteman band from Spring of ‘36 until he died.

ctx.x: Well, Ernie, a sax player, came to me at WINS when WINS, oh, all the networks had live music. Six piece band, eight piece band, forty, whatever. He comes to me and he says, “You know, Al, Benny Bonacchio is going to leave the Whiteman band.” Benny took Chet Haslett’s place, and he’s going to need a first alto player.” I says, “You’ve got to be kidding.” He says, “No, go see him.” So he made an appointment and I went to see him up in Studio 3A, third floor of NBC. This is early 1936. So Paul Whiteman greeted me…
Isn’t that interesting. You see the difference in the ages right there.
